screens.title: The Extract stage explained
screens.narratorSegment: Extraction is the process of retrieving source data so that transformation and loading can proceed. At its core extraction connects to a system—like a relational database, a flat file, or a web A P I—and copies data into a staging area. This sounds simple, but the choice of technique is driven by source size, update frequency, and system constraints. For example, a large operational table should avoid a full daily dump because that can overload the source and waste bandwidth. Instead, incremental extraction uses a last-updated timestamp or an increasing ID to pull only new or modified rows. Extraction also includes a first-pass validation: confirm row counts, a few sample records, and basic types so you catch simple mismatches early. A common misconception is that extraction is a blind copy. In practice, extraction is an informed, efficient pull that anticipates updates, schema changes, and operational limits. Think of extraction as the gatekeeper: it must be accurate, performant, and resilient, because every downstream transformation depends on its quality. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › The Extract stage explained
Definition
What extraction does

Extraction connects to sources and retrieves raw data into a staging area. It is not a passive copy; it must be chosen to match source behavior and operational constraints.

Common sources
  • Relational databases: SELECT queries
  • Flat files: CSV and JSON
  • Web APIs: HTTP JSON endpoints
Real-world check
After extraction verify row counts, inspect a few rows for expected keys and types, and log the extraction time window used.
Analogy
Think of extraction as a dock worker who takes only the crates scheduled for shipment instead of unloading the entire warehouse. Careful selection saves time and resources.
Example scenario
A retail orders table receives thousands of updates daily. A full extract would copy all historical orders every run. Instead, extract rows where order_date is later than the last successful extraction to retrieve only recent activity.
Key Takeaway

Plan extraction with the source in mind, validate the pull, and prefer incremental approaches for large, changing datasets.

screens.title: Full vs Incremental SQL Extraction
screens.narratorSegment: Relational databases are a primary extraction source and the SELECT statement is your main tool. A full extraction pulls all rows and columns from a table. It is simple but often inefficient for large tables. Incremental extraction uses a filter so you retrieve only new or modified rows since the last extraction, commonly by comparing a timestamp column or using an increasing ID range. The chapter gives a clear S Q L example: a full select from orders, and an incremental select where order_date is greater than the last extraction time. A frequent trap is treating incremental extraction as if only inserts occur. If the source updates existing records, you must track a last_modified_timestamp or implement a merge strategy that updates rows in your staging store. When designing incremental queries, ensure the filter column is reliable and indexed on the source to avoid scanning the entire table. Example S Q L helps you see the pattern and practice: use WHERE order_date > 'last_time' or WHERE last_modified_timestamp > 'last_time'. Always record the extraction window so you can re-run or backfill if needed. How will you handle a late-arriving update that changes an earlier row?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Full vs Incremental SQL Extraction
Pattern
Full extraction selects all rows; incremental selects rows newer than a recorded extraction timestamp or within an ID range.
SQL Examples
-- Full extraction (potentially inefficient for large tables)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status
FROM orders;

-- Incremental extraction using a timestamp
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status
FROM orders
WHERE order_date > '2023-10-26 00:00:00'; -- last successful extraction time
Common mistake
Only filtering for new inserts while ignoring updates. If records are updated in place, incremental logic must capture those changes too.
Performance tip
Ensure the column you use for incremental filters is indexed on the source. That prevents full table scans during extraction.
Example scenario
For daily batches of a customer_master table with millions of rows choose incremental extraction based on last_updated_timestamp to avoid transferring the whole table each run.
Key Takeaway

Design your incremental filter carefully and record the extraction window; account for updates as well as inserts.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Extracting CSV files with pandas
Pattern
Use pandas.read_csv inside try-except for clear error reporting and quick inspection with head().
import pandas as pd

# Extracting data from a CSV file
try:
    df_customers = pd.read_csv('customers.csv')
    print("Customers data extracted successfully:")
    print(df_customers.head())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Error: customers.csv not found.")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"An error occurred during CSV extraction: {e}")
Example CSV
customer_id,name,email,registration_date 1,Alice Smith,alice@example.com,2023-01-15 2,Bob Johnson,bob@example.com,2023-02-20
Validation checklist
  • Confirm file exists and opens without encoding errors.
  • Inspect head() for expected columns and types.
  • Compare row count to expected value when available.
Key Takeaway

Wrap file reads in try-except, validate a sample, and avoid loading enormous files into memory without chunking.

Pattern
Use json.load to parse nested structures, then map nested keys into flat fields for staging.
import json

# Extracting data from a JSON file
with open('products.json', 'r') as f:
    products_data = json.load(f)

print("Products data extracted successfully:")
for product in products_data[:2]:  # Print first two products
    print(product)
Example JSON snippet
[{"product_id": "P001", "name": "Laptop", "price": 1200.00, "category": "Electronics"}, ...]
When to normalize
If products contain nested lists or objects, extract the nested structures into separate staging tables and maintain keys to rejoin later.
Key Takeaway

Inspect JSON samples first. Use json.load for nested control and normalize nested objects to maintain a stable schema.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Extracting from Web APIs with requests
Pattern
Use requests.get, call response.raise_for_status, parse response.json(), and handle network exceptions.
import requests

api_url = 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users'  # example mock API

try:
    response = requests.get(api_url)
    response.raise_for_status()
    users_data = response.json()
    print("Users data extracted from API successfully:")
    for user in users_data[:2]:
        print(f"ID: {user['id']}, Name: {user['name']}, Email: {user['email']}")
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print(f"Error during API extraction: {e}")
Test tip
Use a public mock API during development to confirm expected fields, then switch to production endpoints with proper auth tokens and rate-limit handling.
Rate limit strategy
Detect throttling responses and implement retry with backoff. Respect API documentation for safe request patterns.
Key Takeaway

Network extraction must include status checks, exception handling, and respectful retry behavior to be reliable.

screens.title: Full extraction vs Incremental extraction
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between full and incremental extraction is a trade-off between simplicity and efficiency. Full extraction is straightforward: copy everything and start fresh; it can be a reliable recovery mechanism because it re-creates the entire dataset. Incremental extraction is more efficient for large or frequently updated sources because it transfers only new or changed rows. The chapter's assessment highlights a real decision: for a large, continuously updated customer_master table, the correct daily approach is incremental extraction using a last_updated_timestamp, because it limits load on the operational system. Full extraction is tempting for simplicity but becomes impractical at scale. Incremental extraction requires careful bookkeeping: record the last successful extraction timestamp, make sure the filter column is trustworthy and indexed, and design for updates as well as inserts. A common misconception is that incremental means you never need a full refresh; in reality periodic full refreshes or backfills may still be needed to recover from missed windows or schema changes. The core decision rule is: prefer incremental for large, active tables and reserve full extracts for small tables or occasional recovery operations.   • High load and large data transfer for big tables.
Incremental extraction
  • Copies only new/changed rows using timestamps or IDs.
  • Requires tracking the last extraction window and handling updates.
Concrete choice
For a customer_master table with millions of rows and constant updates, choose incremental extraction using a last_updated_timestamp to reduce load on the operational system.
Pitfall
Failing to capture updates when the source modifies existing rows. Use a last_modified_timestamp column or change capture strategy to include updates.
Recovery plan
Keep a process to run a full refresh occasionally or when schema issues require rebuilding the staging table.
Key Takeaway

Balance efficiency with operational safety: incremental for scale, full for recovery and small datasets.

screens.title: Handling schema drift
screens.narratorSegment: Schema drift occurs when a source changes its structure: columns can be added, removed, or change type. If you treat schema as fixed, these changes will break downstream transformations. Detecting schema drift early is essential: inspect keys and data types in a few sample rows after extraction and compare to the expected schema. The chapter suggests flexible ingestion tools or explicit schema validation steps so pipelines can either adapt or fail loudly with actionable logs. A practical pattern is to accept optional new fields and log them for review, while validating required columns and types that your downstream logic expects. When a type changes, for example a numeric ID becoming a string, conversion logic or a schema migration is needed before transformations assume a type. A common misconception is that schema drift is rare; in many operational systems fields are added for new features and your pipeline must be prepared. Build a lightweight schema check that validates presence and type of critical fields and records differences to help you decide whether to auto-accept or pause the pipeline for manual review.

What is schema drift?
A change in the structure or types of source data that can break downstream logic.
Detection steps

screens.title: Performance considerations during extraction
screens.narratorSegment: Performance bottlenecks commonly show up during extraction when naive techniques scan large tables, load huge files into memory, or hammer APIs without regard to rate limits. For databases, ensure the column used for incremental filters is indexed so the query can find new rows without a full scan. For flat files, avoid loading very large CSVs into memory; instead use streaming or chunked reads that process rows in manageable batches. For APIs, check for rate-limiting headers and implement backoff strategies; repeated rapid retries can worsen the situation. The chapter emphasizes logging and monitoring so you can spot extraction slowness and identify the bottleneck. A typical mistake is assuming that a script that works on small test files will scale unchanged. Always test extraction with representative data sizes and observe memory and latency. When possible, negotiate extraction windows with source owners so extracts run during low load and use efficient query patterns. These small operational choices make extractions reliable and cost-effective as data volumes grow. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the Extract stage, the step that supplies all downstream analytics with raw source data. You will learn how to use S Q L to query relational systems efficiently, how to use Python libraries to read CSV and JSON files, and how to request structured data from web APIs. We will contrast full versus incremental extraction and highlight why incremental extraction is often preferred for large, frequently updated tables. You will see concrete examples for a select statement, a pandas CSV read, json parsing, and a simple A P I request. We also cover practical concerns: handling updates to existing rows, schema drift when a source adds or changes columns, performance bottlenecks for very large tables or files, and robust error handling so your pipeline fails gracefully. By the end you will know which extraction technique fits common source types and the first checks to run to validate extracted data. Consider: what would you check first when a daily extraction returns fewer rows than expected?

In this first objectives panel we outline concrete skills you will practice. First, you will implement S Q L queries for efficient extraction from relational databases. That means writing SELECT statements and using WHERE clauses on timestamp or ID columns to limit the data you pull, which matters because full extracts can overload operational systems. Second, you will learn to use Python to read CSV files with pandas. read_csv, including simple error handling for missing files or malformed rows. Practically, this lets you load tabular data into a DataFrame for quick inspection. Third, you will practice parsing JSON files using the json module when data is nested or needs precise control. You will use small examples to see how nested records map to Python structures. Fourth in this screen you will start to distinguish full extraction from incremental extraction, why incremental pulls save time and resources, and when a full refresh is still necessary. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone to help you track progress.

This second objectives panel completes the set of practical skills you'll exercise. First, you will learn to extract data from web APIs using Python's requests library and handle HTTP errors with response checks. This is essential because APIs commonly require authentication and can return rate-limiting errors. Second, you will identify and mitigate common extraction challenges such as schema drift and updates to existing records, learning how schema validation or flexible ingestion prevents pipeline breakage. Third, you will recognize performance bottlenecks and adopt techniques like query optimization, file streaming, and respectful A P I backoff to keep extraction efficient. Finally, you will practice defensive error handling and simple validation steps, using try-except, logging, and row-count checks to ensure data integrity before it proceeds to transformation. Learning Objectives means combine proper error handling, validation, and performance-aware extraction strategies so pipelines run reliably and data integrity is preserved.. In practical terms, skills you will build in this chapter — part 2. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Extraction is the process of retrieving source data so that transformation and loading can proceed. At its core extraction connects to a system—like a relational database, a flat file, or a web A P I—and copies data into a staging area. This sounds simple, but the choice of technique is driven by source size, update frequency, and system constraints. For example, a large operational table should avoid a full daily dump because that can overload the source and waste bandwidth. Instead, incremental extraction uses a last-updated timestamp or an increasing ID to pull only new or modified rows. Extraction also includes a first-pass validation: confirm row counts, a few sample records, and basic types so you catch simple mismatches early. A common misconception is that extraction is a blind copy. In practice, extraction is an informed, efficient pull that anticipates updates, schema changes, and operational limits. Think of extraction as the gatekeeper: it must be accurate, performant, and resilient, because every downstream transformation depends on its quality. Which quick checks will you run immediately after an extraction completes? The Extract stage explained means extraction should be targeted, validated, and resilient — it sets the quality baseline for the entire etl pipeline.. In practical terms, what extraction is, why it matters, and common source types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Relational databases are a primary extraction source and the SELECT statement is your main tool. A full extraction pulls all rows and columns from a table. It is simple but often inefficient for large tables. Incremental extraction uses a filter so you retrieve only new or modified rows since the last extraction, commonly by comparing a timestamp column or using an increasing ID range. The chapter gives a clear S Q L example: a full select from orders, and an incremental select where order_date is greater than the last extraction time. A frequent trap is treating incremental extraction as if only inserts occur. If the source updates existing records, you must track a last_modified_timestamp or implement a merge strategy that updates rows in your staging store. When designing incremental queries, ensure the filter column is reliable and indexed on the source to avoid scanning the entire table. Example S Q L helps you see the pattern and practice: use WHERE order_date > 'last_time' or WHERE last_modified_timestamp > 'last_time'. Always record the extraction window so you can re-run or backfill if needed. How will you handle a late-arriving update that changes an earlier row?

CSV files are one of the most common flat-file sources. The pandas. read_csv function loads a CSV into a DataFrame quickly and provides immediate conveniences like head inspection and basic parsing. The chapter supplies a small code snippet that demonstrates reading a customers CSV file inside a try-except block so a missing file raises a readable error. When working with CSVs, you should peek at the first few rows and check types for key columns, for example dates or numeric amounts. For very large files consider streaming or chunked reads—loading a very large CSV into memory can cause failures. The example also shows handling FileNotFoundError separately from other exceptions so you can report a clear remediation step. In practice, place file paths and credentials in environment variables rather than hardcoding them, and log both success and failure with the row count extracted. A simple example of verification: compare the number of rows you read to an expected count or to a checksum produced by the source. This immediate validation reduces downstream surprises. What quick validation would you add for your CSVs?

JSON files can range from simple flat arrays to deeply nested documents. When your JSON is nested or requires fine-grained control, the json module gives explicit structure: load the file, iterate records, and transform nested keys into the fields you need. The chapter shows a basic json. load example that reads 'products. json' and prints the first few products. If your JSON is tabular, pandas can read it directly, but pandas may not give you the control you need for nested structures. After extraction, inspect the first objects to discover optional or missing keys which can cause schema drift downstream. Always guard file operations with try-except and consider normalizing nested lists into separate tables if needed. A common misconception is that json. load is always slower; in practice it gives clarity for nested shapes and avoids surprising DataFrame flattening. Choosing between full and incremental extraction is a trade-off between simplicity and efficiency. Full extraction is straightforward: copy everything and start fresh; it can be a reliable recovery mechanism because it re-creates the entire dataset. Incremental extraction is more efficient for large or frequently updated sources because it transfers only new or changed rows. The chapter's assessment highlights a real decision: for a large, continuously updated customer_master table, the correct daily approach is incremental extraction using a last_updated_timestamp, because it limits load on the operational system. Full extraction is tempting for simplicity but becomes impractical at scale. Incremental extraction requires careful bookkeeping: record the last successful extraction timestamp, make sure the filter column is trustworthy and indexed, and design for updates as well as inserts. A common misconception is that incremental means you never need a full refresh; in reality periodic full refreshes or backfills may still be needed to recover from missed windows or schema changes. The core decision rule is: prefer incremental for large, active tables and reserve full extracts for small tables or occasional recovery operations. Schema drift occurs when a source changes its structure: columns can be added, removed, or change type. If you treat schema as fixed, these changes will break downstream transformations. Detecting schema drift early is essential: inspect keys and data types in a few sample rows after extraction and compare to the expected schema. The chapter suggests flexible ingestion tools or explicit schema validation steps so pipelines can either adapt or fail loudly with actionable logs. A practical pattern is to accept optional new fields and log them for review, while validating required columns and types that your downstream logic expects. When a type changes, for example a numeric ID becoming a string, conversion logic or a schema migration is needed before transformations assume a type. A common misconception is that schema drift is rare; in many operational systems fields are added for new features and your pipeline must be prepared. Build a lightweight schema check that validates presence and type of critical fields and records differences to help you decide whether to auto-accept or pause the pipeline for manual review.
